UI Design Overview

This prototype adopts a sidebar navigation layout. The left panel contains the key navigation menu and search area, while the main panel is used to display content, visual analytics results, and module-specific outputs.

Input Components

  • Search box
  • Navigation menu
  • Dropdown selection
  • Slider input
  • Checkbox filters

Output Components

  • Interactive charts
  • Summary tables
  • Analytical text outputs
  • Model results
``` ::: ::: ### Description of UI Components The proposed user interface consists of the following major components: 1. **Sidebar navigation panel** The sidebar is used to organize the application into different functional modules. Users can switch between pages such as Home, Project Minutes, Data Preparation, Exploratory Data Analysis, Confirmatory Data Analysis, Cluster Analysis, Decision Tree Analysis, and UI Design. 2. **Search box** The search box is included to improve accessibility and help users quickly locate relevant content or modules within the application. 3. **Main content panel** The main panel is the primary display area for text, plots, analytical outputs, and model results. The displayed content changes according to the selected module. 4. **Input components** Different Shiny input widgets will be used depending on the analytical module, including dropdown menus, sliders, and checkbox filters. 5. **Output components** The output section will present the results of the analysis in the form of charts, tables, explanatory text, and model summaries. ## UI Design for Cluster Analysis Module This section presents the proposed user interface design for the Cluster Analysis module. The purpose of this module is to allow users to explore tourist segmentation patterns interactively by selecting clustering variables and adjusting the number of clusters. ### Storyboard for Cluster Analysis Module ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Description of UI Components for Cluster Analysis The proposed Cluster Analysis module consists of the following key user interface components: 1. **Variable selection input** A dropdown-style selection control is used to allow users to choose the variables included in the clustering procedure, such as age, total spending, and length of stay. 2. **Number of clusters selector** A numeric or slider-based control is used to specify the number of clusters for the k-means clustering model. 3. **Standardization option** A checkbox input is used to indicate whether the selected variables should be standardized before clustering. 4. **Cluster plot output** The main panel contains a visual plot to display clustering results and show how tourists are grouped into distinct segments. 5. **Cluster summary panel** A summary area is included to describe the characteristics of each cluster and improve interpretability. ### Rationale for the Cluster Analysis UI Design The Cluster Analysis module is designed to balance simplicity and interpretability. The sidebar contains only the essential controls required for clustering, while the main panel focuses on presenting the results clearly through a visual plot and a summary panel. This design helps users understand how different parameter selections affect the clustering outcome and supports interactive exploration of tourist segments. ## Cluster Analysis ### Load Packages and Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("pacman") pacman::p_load( tidyverse, dplyr, tidyr, poLCA, janitor, lubridate, scales ) customer_data <- readr::read_csv("data/customer_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) transactions_data <- readr::read_csv("data/transactions_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) ``` ::: The clustering analysis uses both the customer-level dataset and the transaction-level dataset. clustering. Continuous variables such as age, average transaction amount, total transaction count, customer lifetime value, and churn probability were grouped into low, medium, and high categories. Boolean product-ownership indicators were recoded from TRUE/FALSE into 2/1 categories in order to make them compatible with the `poLCA` package. --- ### Latent Class Analysis ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) f <- cbind( gender, income_bracket, education_level, marital_status, acquisition_channel, customer_segment, clv_segment, preferred_transaction_type, dominant_tx_type, age_group, household_group, active_products_group, app_login_group, tx_amount_group, tx_count_group, clv_value_group, churn_group, savings_account, credit_card, personal_loan, investment_account, insurance_product, bill_payment_user, auto_savings_enabled ) ~ 1 calc_entropy <- function(posterior_mat) { n <- nrow(posterior_mat) k <- ncol(posterior_mat) raw_entropy <- -sum(posterior_mat * log(posterior_mat + 1e-12)) 1 - raw_entropy / (n * log(k)) } model_stats <- purrr::map_dfr(2:6, function(k) { m <- poLCA::poLCA( f, data = df_lca, nclass = k, nrep = 5, maxiter = 5000, verbose = FALSE ) tibble::tibble( nclass = k, AIC = m$aic, BIC = m$bic, entropy = calc_entropy(m$posterior) ) }) model_stats ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 4 nclass AIC BIC entropy 1 2 2003397. 2004250. 0.886 2 3 1970941. 1972225. 0.955 3 4 1957490. 1959205. 0.888 4 5 1945855. 1948001. 0.867 5 6 1927217. 1929794. 0.911 ``` ::: ::: Latent Class Analysis (LCA) was used to identify hidden customer segments based on demographic, behavioural, and product-ownership variables. Models with two to six classes were estimated, and their fit was compared using AIC, BIC, and entropy. --- ### Plot BIC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(model_stats, ggplot2::aes(x = nclass, y = BIC)) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#2C7FB8") + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#2C7FB8") + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) + ggplot2::labs( title = "BIC by Number of Classes", x = "Number of Classes", y = "BIC" ) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: BIC was used as the primary criterion for selecting the optimal number of latent classes. A lower BIC indicates a better trade-off between model fit and model complexity. --- ### Plot AIC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(model_stats, ggplot2::aes(x = nclass, y = AIC)) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#D95F0E") + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#D95F0E") + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) + ggplot2::labs( title = "AIC by Number of Classes", x = "Number of Classes", y = "AIC" ) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: AIC was also examined as a secondary fit criterion. In general, lower AIC values indicate improved model fit, although AIC tends to prefer slightly more complex models than BIC. --- ### Plot Entropy ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(model_stats, ggplot2::aes(x = nclass, y = entropy)) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#238B45") + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#238B45") + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) + ggplot2::labs( title = "Entropy by Number of Classes", x = "Number of Classes", y = "Entropy" ) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Entropy measures how clearly the observations are assigned to latent classes. Higher entropy indicates better class separation and greater certainty in class membership. --- ### Final Model Selection ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best_k <- model_stats %>% dplyr::filter(BIC == financial product ownership, transaction behaviour, and customer value indicators. For example, one cluster may represent highly engaged customers with multiple financial products, frequent app usage, and high customer lifetime value. Another cluster may represent low-engagement customers with fewer products, lower transaction activity, and higher churn risk. A third cluster may reflect medium-value transactional customers with moderate product adoption and stable behavioural patterns. These latent classes are useful for identifying differentiated customer strategies, such as retention campaigns for high-risk customers, cross-selling opportunities for medium-engagement customers, and loyalty programmes for high-value customer groups.
